pillar_reactions.evidence: Understood immediately, agreed, and had no questions — 'I already watched all the videos as well.' He was pre-sold on the modality from his own history: 'I know what working out with kettlebells can do, because I really was very healthy there.' When the mobility protocols were presented he answered by describing the routine he already runs — hourly walking breaks, a standing desk two to three times a day for 15-25 minutes, daily wall stretches for volleyball — and closed with 'So I'm already implementing a lot of those things already.' Accepted rather than enthusiastic: the pillar told him nothing he was not already doing.

The only substantive pushback of the call, and it went to the core of the pillar. On the rep's suggestion that he might be under-eating he said flatly 'eating more I tried it, and then I was gaining weight.' He then rejected the pillar's central premise — that fullness self-regulates on whole foods — with his own physiology: 'My only problem or the thing that I can foresee as a program are those cravings... if I let loose, I can eat up to 18,000 calories. I tested it. I tried. And I still didn't cause a feeling of full. So that's how broken my system is.' He also described the workarounds he has already engineered for himself, foods that expand in the stomach with water, which is a more sophisticated answer than the protocol offered. The rep deferred rather than resolved: 'I don't want to step into Trevor's shoes right now, because he's way more experienced in that.'

Agreed without friction and with no enthusiasm. The rep pre-empted the pillar by conceding he probably does not need it — 'from what I see from you, you're a very disciplined guy. You don't need to be hand-holded, but the coaching layer matters because life gets busy' — and the prospect's only contribution was to extend the failure mode from workouts to sleep: 'Or skip sleep, yeah, yeah.' He asked no questions about the app, the check-ins or the form corrections. His follow-up questions were about programme fit for autism and ADHD, not about the accountability mechanics.

anchors.raw: I can tell you that everything above 200 euros a month is too much for me, even with my current job.
anchors.note: A hard ceiling stated in euros against a price quoted in dollars, roughly a quarter of what the six-month programme requires per month. He volunteered it immediately and without prompting, and added that it will fall further if his next job pays less. The rep took the number at face value and disqualified — correctly — but it arrived at minute 54 of a 60-minute call, which is the real cost.

anchors.raw: For $200 a month, what I could offer you is the Primal University, which is Trevor's community group... And that is $199 per month. And you can cancel that anytime.
anchors.note: First appearance in the corpus of the Primal University price and terms, offered live as a downsell. It is priced within a dollar of the prospect's stated ceiling, which made it feel bespoke rather than standard. Worth tracking across the corpus: a cancel-anytime $199/month product sitting under a $6,000 six-month programme is a permanent anchor against every full-price close, and the Daniel call the same day shows a prospect finding it on his own before the price conversation.

anchors.raw: I'm paying a lot already with the CLI program that I have to follow, and the dieticians, well, that's all things that you have to follow by Dutch health insurance laws
anchors.competitor: Dutch CLI combined lifestyle intervention and a dietitian
anchors.note: He is already enrolled in a state-adjacent, insurance-funded lifestyle intervention with a clinical dietitian, entered on his family doctor's referral. That is a functioning low-cost substitute with clinical credibility the programme does not have, and it was never addressed. It also means a clinician is already directing his nutrition, which nobody on the call attempted to coordinate with.

anchors.raw: here, credit card systems work differently than in other countries. I don't know if you know the difference, but you have to actually pay it back directly or with huge kind of interests, and those interests are around 14% every month. So that's a lot. So that's why everyone's paying it directly.
anchors.note: Structural rather than personal, and the most transferable finding on the call. The playbook's money play assumes a revolving credit card is the default instrument — 'most of the guys put it on a credit card upfront' — which does not exist in the same form in the Netherlands. Any Dutch or wider European prospect faces this, and the script has no alternative to offer.

anchors.raw: am I going for that? Or am I going to my local physician and ask them to give me one-on-one training? Because I want to get better.
anchors.note: The real competitor for this budget is not another online coach, it is an in-person clinician who can also handle the back, the IBS and the eating disorder. The rep did not contest the comparison. Given the clinical picture, an in-person clinician is arguably the better product, which is a positioning problem rather than a rep failure.

anchors.raw: I was also considering reaching out to someone in the UK, I think you know him, he's with that Razor program... I think it's the injury that tilts the coin to his side instead of the UK guy's side.
anchors.note: He shopped the category and chose Trevor before the call, on the strength of Trevor's back injury mirroring his own slipped disc. Useful marketing intelligence: the injury story, not the physique, is what converted a comparison shopper. The rep did not ask what the UK alternative costs.

unmet_demand.want: A nutrition approach that works for someone with no satiety signal at all — 'I still didn't cause a feeling of full. So that's how broken my system is.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The nutrition pillar rests on the claim that 'it's virtually impossible to overeat when you're eating real food' and that the how-much variable 'takes care of itself'. That mechanism is exactly the one this prospect's body does not have, following a congenital malformation uncorrected until age three. The offer's central nutritional premise is inapplicable to him, and the rep's answer was to defer to Trevor rather than to address it.

unmet_demand.want: A coach with knowledge of appetite and food dysregulation in autism, ADHD and diagnosed bulimia nervosa
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Asked directly, the rep answered honestly that he does not know whether Trevor has that knowledge. Nobody on the call could establish it either way, and there is no clinical intake that would. This should be escalated to a human rather than assumed in either direction — and if the answer is no, an intermittent-fasting protocol should not be presented to prospects with a diagnosed eating disorder.

unmet_demand.want: Something between $199/month of community content and $6,000 for six months of one-to-one
unmet_demand.why_unmet: There is nothing in between. His ceiling was €200/month, which is roughly €1,200 over six months against a €5,000-plus gap — but the shape of the gap matters more than the size: he is a genuinely high-intent, high-discipline prospect who is currently disqualified into a self-serve product he has already told you cannot solve his actual problem.

unmet_demand.want: A way to pay that does not depend on a revolving credit card
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Dutch credit cards require immediate repayment or carry roughly 14% monthly interest. The programme's stated norm is upfront on a card, and the only alternative offered was an unspecified 'split' that was never structured. No SEPA direct debit, iDEAL, or instalment mechanism was mentioned.

unmet_demand.want: Coordination with the clinicians already treating him — a family doctor, a dietitian and a CLI programme
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Never raised by either side. The programme has no mechanism for working alongside an existing clinical team, and on this call that would have been both the safest and the most persuasive move available: he is already being told what to eat by a dietitian on referral.
